slides: Support by comparison.
In a comparison, we compare our case to some other field. And we want the two to share as many characteristics as possible.
Why? Because it's a kind of analogy. I want to draw a conclusion about our case from the case I'm about to describe.
It doesn't have to be identical. Not cameras and security again. But it has to be similar enough.
Otherwise someone can say: wait, that's not comparable. You're showing me some other field, but you can't compare them. There, lots of other things are different.
So ask yourself: the feature that makes it work there... is it also here? That's the part of the comparison that has to match.
Now, finding another field that's really similar isn't easy. It takes very high-level critical thinking.
So if you don't feel strong at this, don't take the risk. Stay with an example.
An example is easier. You invent a likely story about our own case. In a comparison you also tell a story, but it has to be about a similar field. And sometimes you drift too far.
So here's the same start of the paragraph. Same key sentence, same development. And now, a comparison.
I took a different case. There are workplaces with computers, and the employees know they're not allowed to use them for personal things.
If the computers weren't monitored, an employee might think: nobody can catch me. I'll browse, and check my personal messages.
But once the company tells them, our computers are monitored, activity is recorded, we'll know... then they think: okay, in that case, I'll probably cut down on personal use at work.
So far it sounds logical, and it's something we all know. And the shared feature is exactly the one our argument needs. People know they're recorded, so they change their behaviour.
But wait. I've been talking about computers and messages. What does that have to do with our cameras?
So I connect it back, with my closing link. In the same way, awareness of the cameras in public spaces is likely to deter offenders from acting in these areas.
Just as employees who know they're monitored cut down, offenders who know certain areas are monitored are likely to cut down too. Or even stop completely.
Writing this closing link well isn't simple. I really recommend you practise it.
There's a danger here. A lot of students write a closing sentence that just repeats. They go over their whole argument again, without actually connecting it to the example or the comparison.
That's padding. And that's not the goal.
The goal is to explain the connection. In the same way. Or, like with the example: just as the pickpocket, so other offenders.
So, a quick test. Does your closing link mention both the support case and your own case? If it only repeats your argument, rewrite it.
